deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is a page of Riemann's 1847 student essay 'Versuch einer allgemeinen Auffassung der Integration und Differentiation', printed posthumously in the Werke (1876). The notation is as follows. ^x∂^ν z (written ∂^ν_x z in the transcription) is a derivative of index ν. Π(s)=Γ(s+1). Law (3) is the generalized binomial expansion (x+h)^α/Π(α) = Σ_n x^n/Πn · h^(α−n)/Π(α−n). The defining requirement is z(x+h) = Σ_ν ^x∂^ν z · h^ν/Πν, with ν running through ν0+ℤ, under the side condition that each coefficient is the x-derivative of the preceding one.

(A) Uniqueness: a value p_ν of ∂^ν z belongs to only one development.
- Suppose p_ν belongs to developments a (terms p) and b (terms q). All later terms agree, because they are derivatives of p_ν.
- Since dq_{ν−1}/dx = dp_{ν−1}/dx = p_ν, we get q_{ν−1} = p_{ν−1} + k_1.
- Integrating repeatedly gives q_{ν−2} = p_{ν−2} + k_1 x + k_2 and q_{ν−3} = p_{ν−3} + k_1 x²/2! + k_2 x + k_3.
- In general q_{ν−m} = p_{ν−m} + Σ_{j=1}^m k_j x^{m−j}/(m−j)!.
- Hence b − a = Σ_m h^{ν−m}/Π(ν−m) Σ_j k_j x^{m−j}/(m−j)!. Regrouping by j, with n = m−j, gives Σ_j k_j Σ_{n≥0} x^n/n! · h^{ν−j−n}/Π(ν−j−n).
- By (3) this equals Σ_j k_j (x+h)^{ν−j}/Π(ν−j).
- Both developments equal z(x+h), so this must vanish for all x+h. Riemann concludes ('bekanntlich') that all k_j = 0, so a and b coincide.

(B) Complementary terms.
- If p_ν is a value, so is p_ν + k x^{−ν−n}/Π(−ν−n), for n a positive integer.
- Summed against h^ν/Πν, the added terms give, by (3) with x and h exchanged, k (x+h)^{−n}/Π(−n). This is 0 because 1/Γ(1−n) = 0. So the series still represents z(x+h).
- The derivative law is preserved, since d/dx[x^{−ν−n}/Π(−ν−n)] = x^{−ν−n−1}/Π(−ν−n−1).
- All values obtainable from one another by adding such terms form a 'System'. Formula (6) gives the whole system: p_ν + Σ_{n≥1} k_n x^{−ν−n}/Π(−ν−n). This is Riemann's well-known 'complementary function'.

(C) Construction of one value.
- Start from Taylor's series z(x) = Σ_j z^{(j)}(k)(x−k)^j/j!, valid when z is continuous between k and x.
- Replace x by x+h. Expand each ((x−k)+h)^j/j! by (3) in powers h^μ, with μ ∈ ν0+ℤ.
- This gives z(x+h) = Σ_μ h^μ/Πμ · ^k p_μ, where ^k p_μ = Σ_{j≥0} z^{(j)}(k) (x−k)^{j−μ}/Π(j−μ).
- d/dx ^k p_{μ−1} = ^k p_μ termwise, so ^k p_μ is an admissible value of ∂^μ z.
- (On the next page this is identified, for μ<0, with the Riemann–Liouville integral (1/Γ(−μ))∫_k^x (x−t)^{−μ−1} z(t) dt. Termwise this follows from the Beta integral; this check is mine.)
errors: Riemann writes the left side of the Taylor-derived expansion as z_x. It should be z_{x+h}, since x+h was substituted for x.
In (B) he writes the sum of the added terms as k x^{−n}/Π(−n). By (3) it is k (x+h)^{−n}/Π(−n). Both vanish because 1/Π(−n)=0 for positive integer n, so the conclusion is unaffected.

The uniqueness argument is not rigorous on three points. It assumes convergence and rearrangement of doubly infinite series. It relies on (3), which converges only for |x|<|h|. It invokes 'bekanntlich' an identity theorem for series in powers (x+h)^{ν−m} with exponents unbounded below.
For integer ν the uniqueness argument fails. Then 1/Π(ν−m)=0 for m>ν, so the constants k_m with m>ν drop out and remain undetermined. This is precisely the polynomial ambiguity of repeated integrals.
The complementary function (6) has an infinite sum of arbitrary constants. Its convergence is not discussed. This ambiguity was later criticized (Cayley 1880).

results.what: Uniqueness of the development of z(x+h) in fractional powers of h to which a given value of the ν-th derivative belongs, under the condition that successive coefficients are derivatives
results.modern_name: Fractional Taylor series / generalized Taylor expansion (uniqueness lemma)

results.what: Ambiguity of fractional derivatives by terms k x^{−ν−n}/Γ(1−ν−n); the notion of a 'system of values'

Construction of a fractional derivative via Taylor series about k combined with the generalized binomial theorem: Σ_j z^{(j)}(k)(x−k)^{j−μ}/Γ(j−μ+1), equal to the Riemann–Liouville integral with lower limit k

deep.surprise_reason: This page belongs to Riemann's 1847 essay on generalized differentiation. It is printed in his Gesammelte Werke (1876), and the Riemann–Liouville integral and complementary function are named after this very work.

checkable.asserts: The complementary term obeys the derivative law: d/dx x^{-ν-n}/Π(-ν-n) = x^{-ν-n-1}/Π(-ν-n-1).
1/Π(-n)=0 for positive integers n, so the added complementary series sums to 0.
Law (3), the generalized binomial (x+h)^α/Π(α)=Σ x^n/n! h^{α-n}/Π(α-n), checked numerically with x=1/2, h=2, α=1/3 (result ≈ 0).
The Beta integral ∫_k^x (x-t)^{a-1}(t-k)^j/j! dt = Γ(a)(x-k)^{j+a}/Γ(j+a+1), linking ^k p_μ (μ=-a) to the Riemann–Liouville integral.
The coefficient of h^μ/Πμ is the x-derivative of the coefficient of h^{μ-1}/Π(μ-1), checked termwise.

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'q_{ν-1}=p_{ν-1}+k_1x' should read q_{ν-1}=p_{ν-1}+k_1. The x in the image appears struck out, and only a constant is mathematically correct.
Notations 'Π-ν-n' and 'Π-n' mean Π(-ν-n) and Π(-n).
'∂^ν_x z' renders Riemann's ^x∂^ν_z (derivative of order ν with respect to x).
'Π\mu-1' in the last lines should be Π(μ-1).
The left side 'z_x' of the final series is as written in the image, but it is Riemann's slip for z_{x+h}.
'^kp_μ' in the last line is ^k p_μ, i.e. p_μ with a left superscript k indicating the base point.
